## Why One Separating Line Is Not Enough

Suppose we want to separate two groups of points. We label them $+1$ and $-1$. Many lines may classify every training point correctly. The next question is how to choose among them.

A support vector machine looks for a large gap between the classes. This gap is called the **margin**. It gives the boundary some room before a small change in a point changes its predicted class.

This is a useful design rule. It is not a promise that the largest training margin always gives the best predictions. The data, the features, and the choice of regularisation still matter.

The main aim of these notes is to connect the geometry with the optimisation. The numerical example below was constructed for these notes.

## Scores, Boundaries, and Distances

For an input $x\in\mathbb R^d$, define the score

$$
f(x)=w^\top x+b,
$$

where $w\ne0$. The decision boundary is the hyperplane $w^\top x+b=0$. Positive scores predict $+1$. Negative scores predict $-1$. A zero score is a tie.

The vector $w$ points across the boundary at a right angle. Its direction matters for the boundary. Its length changes the scale of the scores.

To see the distance formula, move from $x$ in the direction $w/\lVert w\rVert$. Write a point on this line as

$$
x-t\frac{w}{\lVert w\rVert}.
$$

It lies on the boundary when

$$
w^\top x+b-t\lVert w\rVert=0.
$$

Thus the signed distance to the boundary is

$$
\frac{w^\top x+b}{\lVert w\rVert}.
$$

The ordinary distance is its absolute value. A score alone is not a geometric distance. We must divide by $\lVert w\rVert$.

## Why We Can Set the Score Margin to One

Multiplying $w$ and $b$ by the same positive constant leaves all predicted signs unchanged. It also leaves the boundary unchanged. So a larger raw score does not, by itself, mean a better classifier.

For strictly separable data, we can scale the parameters so that

$$
\min_i y_i(w^\top x_i+b)=1.
$$

This puts the nearest training points on the two supporting planes

$$
w^\top x+b=1
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
w^\top x+b=-1.
$$

Each plane is $1/\lVert w\rVert$ from the boundary. Their total separation is therefore

$$
\frac{2}{\lVert w\rVert}.
$$

Some books call the half-width the margin. Here, “margin width” means the full gap. Both conventions lead to the same optimisation problem.

## The Hard-Margin Problem

The training data are $(x_i,y_i)$ for $i=1,\ldots,n$. The hard-margin problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min_{w,b}\quad &\frac12\lVert w\rVert^2\\
\text{subject to}\quad &y_i(w^\top x_i+b)\ge1,
\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.
\end{aligned}
$$

Minimising the squared norm maximises the margin width. The factor $1/2$ makes derivatives simpler. It does not change the minimiser.

The objective is convex. The constraints are affine inequalities. This is a convex quadratic programme. Every local minimum is global, although that fact alone does not tell us how much computation is needed.

Hard-margin training needs separable data. If the two classes overlap, these constraints may have no feasible solution.

### A One-Dimensional Example

Take $x_1=-3$ with label $-1$ and $x_2=5$ with label $+1$. The constraints become

$$
3w-b\ge1,
\qquad
5w+b\ge1.
$$

Adding them gives $8w\ge2$, so $w\ge1/4$. The smallest possible norm occurs at $w=1/4$ and $b=-1/4$. The score is $(x-1)/4$, so the boundary is $x=1$.

Each training point is four units from the boundary. The full margin width is $2/(1/4)=8$. This agrees with the distance between $-3$ and $5$.

This example shows why the constraints are essential. Minimising the norm without them would simply give $w=0$.

## From the Primal to the Dual

The [notes on duality](duality-kkt.qmd) explain the general method. Here, write each constraint as $1-y_i(w^\top x_i+b)\le0$. Introduce multipliers $\alpha_i\ge0$:

$$
L(w,b,\alpha)=\frac12\lVert w\rVert^2
+\sum_i\alpha_i\bigl[1-y_i(w^\top x_i+b)\bigr].
$$

To find the infimum over $w$ and $b$, differentiate:

$$
\nabla_wL=w-\sum_i\alpha_i y_i x_i=0,
\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial b}=-\sum_i\alpha_i y_i=0.
$$

Hence

$$
w=\sum_i\alpha_i y_i x_i,
\qquad
\sum_i\alpha_i y_i=0.
$$

Substitute the first expression back into $L$. The terms containing $w$ combine to give $-\lVert w\rVert^2/2$. The dual problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max_{\alpha}\quad &\sum_i\alpha_i
-\frac12\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_j y_i y_j x_i^\top x_j\\
\text{subject to}\quad &\alpha_i\ge0,
\qquad \sum_i\alpha_i y_i=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

The primal minimises a convex objective. The dual maximises a concave objective. These are consistent directions, not competing definitions of the same problem.

Strict separability gives a strictly feasible point after scaling. The usual strong-duality conditions therefore hold for this hard-margin problem.

## Why Support Vectors Matter

Complementary slackness gives

$$
\alpha_i\bigl[y_i(w^\top x_i+b)-1\bigr]=0.
$$

If $\alpha_i>0$, the corresponding training point lies on a supporting plane. Such points are called **support vectors**. They enter the expression for $w$.

If a point lies strictly beyond the margin, its constraint has room to spare. Complementary slackness then forces $\alpha_i=0$. It makes no direct contribution to the fitted decision rule.

The converse needs care. A point can lie on a supporting plane and still have a zero multiplier in a degenerate solution.

For a hard-margin support vector, we can recover the intercept from

$$
b=y_i-w^\top x_i.
$$

In the two-point example, the dual constraint gives $\alpha_1=\alpha_2=a$. Then $w=8a$, and the dual objective is $2a-32a^2$. Its maximum occurs at $a=1/32$. This gives $w=1/4$, as before.

Using the positive support vector, $b=1-5/4=-1/4$. Both the primal and dual objective values are $1/32$. The numerical answer therefore checks the geometry, stationarity, and strong duality together.

## Soft Margins and Imperfect Data

Real data often overlap or contain unusual points. Introduce slack variables $\xi_i\ge0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min_{w,b,\xi}\quad &\frac12\lVert w\rVert^2+C\sum_i\xi_i\\
\text{subject to}\quad &y_i(w^\top x_i+b)\ge1-\xi_i,\\
&\xi_i\ge0,
\end{aligned}
$$

where $C>0$. At an optimum, the smallest feasible slack is used:

$$
\xi_i=\max\{0,1-y_i f(x_i)\}.
$$

This is the **hinge loss**. A point can be classified correctly and still have positive loss. A score gap between zero and one is on the correct side, but inside the desired margin.

Larger $C$ makes each unit of margin violation more costly. Smaller $C$ puts relatively more weight on a small norm. Validation data help choose the trade-off. SVMs are also sensitive to feature scales, so the same feature scaling must be used during training and prediction (scikit-learn developers, n.d.).

## The Soft-Margin Dual

The same derivation gives the same dual objective, with one extra bound:

$$
0\le\alpha_i\le C.
$$

The upper bound comes from stationarity in $\xi_i$. If $\mu_i\ge0$ is the multiplier for $-\xi_i\le0$, then

$$
C-\alpha_i-\mu_i=0.
$$

The KKT conditions give a useful picture:

| Multiplier | What It Implies |
|---|---|
| $\alpha_i=0$ | The point is on or beyond the margin; it has no direct term in $w$. |
| $0<\alpha_i<C$ | The point is exactly on the margin, with $y_i f(x_i)=1$. |
| $\alpha_i=C$ | The point is on or inside the margin; it may be misclassified. |

An upper-bound multiplier does not prove that a point is wrong. It may still have a positive score with a small margin. To compute $b$ from the margin equality, use a point with $0<\alpha_i<C$ when one is available.

## What This Changes About the Geometry

The hard-margin model asks for perfect separation. The soft-margin model asks whether a wider, simpler boundary is worth a few violations. It balances two goals instead of treating every difficult point as a fixed obstacle.

The dual also changes how we view the data. The prediction score is

$$
f(x)=\sum_i\alpha_i y_i x_i^\top x+b.
$$

Only inner products appear. This observation leads directly to [feature maps and kernels](kernels.qmd).

For the multiclass extension, see [the Crammer-Singer project](../../projects/multiclass-svm-crammer-singer.qmd). It applies the margin idea to several competing class scores.
